title: Daytime shelter procurement and location scoring
subtitle: Also: Ward 6 vacancy, climate action requests to the province, social media code of conduct, 2024 year-end finances.
overview: Council directed staff to run a competitive procurement for daytime shelter services and report back through the 2026 budget update {{vote:m20}}. Council asked the Mayor to include funding in that update and asked the County of Wellington to pay 10 per cent as a discretionary social service. The RFP will give a higher location score to proposals outside several named downtown main streets, will require detailed operating information from bidders, and will give points for easy access to Guelph Transit.

Council also declared the Ward 6 seat vacant {{vote:m23}} and chose an open call for nominations to fill it, with a special meeting on July 23, 2025 {{vote:m24}}. It approved a revised Code of Conduct with new rules on moderating and blocking people on social media {{vote:m27}}. It asked the province to require heat pumps and adopt a tiered energy performance standard for new buildings {{vote:m22}}.

Council made seven sets of advisory committee appointments {{vote:m8}}. The consent report covered the 2024 year-end operating and capital budget results and the reserves and debt statement. After a closed session on the shelter item, the Mayor reported that staff received legal advice and council gave no direction.

decisions.detail: Staff will run a competitive procurement for daytime shelter services and report back through the 2026 budget update, with the Mayor asked to include funding and the County asked to pay 10 per cent.

The RFP will score proposals higher when they are not on Wyndham Street (between Wellington and Woolwich), Carden, Quebec, Cork Street E, Macdonell or Wilson Streets, without barring any location {{vote:m12}}.
Bidders must provide details on the location, accessibility, staffing and training, safe operations, codes of conduct, a good neighbour approach and washroom access {{vote:m13}}.
The Clerk will run an open call for nominations, a special council meeting on July 23, 2025 will make the appointment, and the Council Vacancy Policy is approved.

The revised Code of Conduct is approved with amendments on social media: members who run a public forum cannot exclude critics, should use restraint in blocking, and must moderate abusive or hateful comments.

decisions.item: Requests to the province on building energy
decisions.detail: Council asked Ontario to amend the Building Code to promote heat pumps and to adopt a tiered energy standard for net-zero-ready new buildings by 2030 or sooner.
Council approved staff actions to support collective community climate action.
Residents were appointed to seven advisory committees, and the Clerk will keep recruiting for remaining vacancies.

debate: Most delegates on the shelter item supported a daytime shelter but urged that it be downtown. They said people would stay near meals, pharmacies and other services, carry belongings, and face hills and limited transit elsewhere. Several opposed any location restrictions or scoring.

Delegates and one councilor said location preferences and extra requirements could deter bidders, add delay and cost, and penalize existing downtown providers. Staff said most of the proposed requirements are standard RFP content, and that more scope can raise proposal costs and could affect how many bids arrive.

Supporters of the location scoring said it was a preference and not a restriction, and that anyone could still apply. They said it aimed to balance social services with retail vibrancy on the main downtown streets. One councilor supported the proposal requirements but not the location scoring, while another did the reverse. One councilor called the requirements operational and an overreach for politicians.

Proposed extra scoring on slopes, areas of highest need, Welcoming Streets and nearby services was defeated. Councillors said it was too prescriptive and that staff already weigh these factors. Staff said two more location-based scores could cancel each other out.

On the social media code, a councillor said the first two changes came from the integrity commissioner and the third adds a duty to moderate hateful comments. Others asked who decides what is hateful, and staff noted the duty is a rare positive obligation in the code.
